title: Statistics for Data Science and AI
subtitle: Describe data, reason with probability, and test ideas with confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, regression and A/B tests, in Python with pandas and SciPy.
outcomes: Summarise a dataset's centre, spread and shape with pandas, and investigate its outliers
Calculate probabilities with the binomial, Poisson and normal distributions in SciPy
Explain sampling distributions and the central limit theorem, and build confidence intervals
Run and interpret t-tests and chi-square tests, and avoid the common traps with p-values
Measure relationships with correlation and simple linear regression
Analyse an A/B test and work out how many users it needs
prerequisites: Basic Python: variables, functions, lists and running a script (Python Programming with PyCharm covers it), and school maths. Install PyCharm (the free version is enough) and Python 3; you'll install pandas and SciPy into a project's virtual environment in the first lesson.
description: Data science and AI are built on statistics: every model is fitted to a sample, every evaluation is an estimate, and every claim that one version beats another is a test. In this course you learn the statistics behind those decisions by doing it in Python. You'll describe data with pandas, from means and medians to quartiles and outliers; reason about chance with the binomial, Poisson and normal distributions in SciPy; see the central limit theorem happen in a simulation; and build confidence intervals and hypothesis tests that say how sure you can be. You'll also learn what p-values don't tell you, measure relationships with correlation and regression, and analyse an A/B test, including how many users it needs before it starts. Every lesson is shown in PyCharm, with the Python Console, the debugger and the docs at your fingertips, every module ends with a lab on made-up sample data that comes with the course, and the course ends with a project in which you analyse a field trial and write up what it does and doesn't show.

modules.title: Describing data
modules.summary: Summarise a dataset before you model it: the kinds of data, the centre, the spread and the shape, outliers, and how groups differ, with pandas in PyCharm.

lessons.title: Kinds of data, and where the middle is
objectives: Tell numerical data from categorical data
Choose between the mean, the median and the mode
key_points: Numerical data are measured or counted, such as delivery minutes or items in an order; categorical data put things into groups, such as zone or vehicle; ordinal data are categories with an order, such as small, medium and large.
The mean is the sum divided by the count; the median is the middle value once the data are sorted; the mode is the most common value, and the only one of the three that works for categories.
A few very large values pull the mean up but barely move the median, so in right-skewed data, such as delivery times or incomes, the mean is above the median.
pandas reads a CSV file into a DataFrame with pd.read_csv; each column is a Series, with methods such as .mean(), .median() and .mode(), and .value_counts() counts each category.

Look before you calculate: df.head() shows the first rows, df.shape the number of rows and columns, and df.dtypes each column's type. A numeric ID column is a label, not a measurement, so its mean means nothing.

lessons.title: Spread, quartiles and outliers
objectives: Measure spread with the range, the standard deviation and the interquartile range
Flag outliers with the 1.5 x IQR rule and decide what to do with them
key_points: The range is the maximum minus the minimum, so one extreme value sets it. The standard deviation is roughly the typical distance of values from the mean, and the variance is its square.
pandas' .std() and .var() divide by n - 1, giving the sample standard deviation, by default; NumPy's np.std divides by n unless you pass ddof=1.

Quartiles split sorted data into four equal parts: Q1 is the 25th percentile, the median the 50th and Q3 the 75th. The interquartile range, IQR = Q3 - Q1, is the spread of the middle half, and extreme values don't affect it.

A common rule flags values below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR as outliers. An outlier is a value to investigate, not to delete automatically: it may be an error, or the most important case in the data.
df.describe() gives the count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles and maximum of every numeric column in one table.

lessons.title: Comparing groups
objectives: Summarise a variable for each group with groupby
Compare groups fairly, looking at spread and counts as well as averages
key_points: df.groupby('zone')['minutes'].agg(['count', 'mean', 'median', 'std']) gives a summary table with one row for each group.
Compare groups on their spread and their sizes as well as their averages: a small group's mean can change a lot when one value changes.
pd.crosstab(df['zone'], df['vehicle']) counts each combination of two categories; normalize='index' turns the counts into proportions within each row.
A z-score, (x - mean) / SD, says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean, which puts values measured on different scales side by side.
A difference between groups in the data you have may be chance; later modules show how to judge that with confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.

modules.title: Probability and distributions
modules.summary: Reason about chance: the rules of probability, conditional probability, and the binomial, Poisson and normal distributions, calculated with SciPy and checked by simulation.

lessons.title: Probability rules and conditional probability
objectives: Apply the complement, addition and multiplication rules
Calculate a conditional probability from a table of data
key_points: A probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). The probabilities of all the possible outcomes add up to 1, so P(not A) = 1 - P(A).
For events that can't happen together, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B); in general, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
The conditional probability of A given B, P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B), is the probability of A counting only the cases where B happened.
A and B are independent when knowing one tells you nothing about the other: then P(A | B) = P(A), and P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).
P(A | B) is usually not P(B | A): the chance that a van delivery is late is not the chance that a late delivery was made by van.
With data, a proportion estimates a probability: the mean of a True/False column is the share of True values, and grouping first gives a conditional probability for each group.

lessons.title: Counting successes: the binomial and Poisson distributions
objectives: Recognise when the binomial or the Poisson distribution fits
Calculate probabilities with scipy.stats and check them by simulation
key_points: A random variable gives a number to each outcome of a chance process; a discrete one takes separate, countable values, such as the number of seeds that germinate.
The binomial distribution counts successes in n independent trials that each succeed with the same probability p; its mean is n x p and its variance n x p x (1 - p).

The Poisson distribution counts events in a fixed interval when they happen independently at a steady average rate, such as calls to a help desk in an hour; its mean and its variance both equal that rate.
In scipy.stats, pmf(k) gives P(X = k), cdf(k) gives P(X <= k) and sf(k) gives P(X > k), so P(X >= 8) is sf(7).

Simulation checks a calculation: with rng = np.random.default_rng(42), rng.binomial(10, 0.8, size=100_000) gives 100,000 simulated counts, and the share meeting a condition approaches its probability as the number of simulations grows.

lessons.title: The normal distribution
objectives: Describe the normal distribution and the 68-95-99.7 rule
Find probabilities and percentiles with cdf and ppf
key_points: The normal distribution is the symmetric bell curve set by its mean and standard deviation. Many measurements are roughly normal, though plenty, such as delivery times and incomes, are skewed.
About 68% of a normal distribution lies within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2 and 99.7% within 3.
For a continuous variable, a probability is an area under the curve: stats.norm(loc=mean, scale=sd).cdf(x) gives P(X <= x), and P(a < X <= b) is cdf(b) - cdf(a).
ppf is the inverse of cdf: ppf(0.9) is the 90th percentile, the value with 90% of the distribution below it.

The standard normal distribution has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and a z-score converts any normal value to it, which is why stats.norm.cdf(1) - stats.norm.cdf(-1) is the share within 1 SD of any normal distribution.

steps.do: In a new file, normal.py, model plot yields as normal with mean 2.6 and SD 0.5 tonnes per hectare, and find the share below 2.0.
steps.code:
from scipy import stats

yields = stats.norm(loc=2.6, scale=0.5)
print(yields.cdf(2.0))

steps.do: Add the share between 2.0 and 3.0 and the 90th percentile, then run the file.
steps.code:

print(yields.ppf(0.90))

steps.code:
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    print(k, stats.norm.cdf(k) - stats.norm.cdf(-k))

steps.see: 0.6827, 0.9545 and 0.9973 appear one by one in the Debug console.

modules.title: From samples to conclusions
modules.summary: Go from a sample to the population it came from: the central limit theorem, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and the traps that make p-values mislead.

lessons.title: Samples, sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
objectives: Explain what a sampling distribution is
State the central limit theorem and use the standard error
key_points: A population is everything you want to know about; a sample is the part you measure. A statistic, such as a sample mean, estimates a population parameter, such as the population mean.

A sample represents its population only if it's chosen without bias, ideally at random; a convenient or self-selected sample, such as the people who chose to answer a survey, can mislead however large it is.
Different samples give different means. The sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic over all the samples you could have drawn.

The central limit theorem: for large enough samples of independent values, the sampling distribution of the mean is close to normal even when the population is skewed, provided the population's variance is finite.
The standard deviation of the sample mean, the standard error, is sigma / sqrt(n), so four times the data halves it. With data you estimate it as s / sqrt(n), which scipy.stats.sem computes.

walkthrough.title: Watch the central limit theorem happen

steps.do: In a new file, clt.py, make a skewed population of 100,000 waiting times averaging 10 minutes.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
population = rng.exponential(scale=10, size=100_000)
print(population.mean(), population.std(), stats.skew(population))

steps.do: Draw 2,000 samples of 30, keep each sample's mean, and summarise the means.
steps.code:
n = 30
means = np.array([rng.choice(population, size=n).mean() for _ in range(2_000)])
print(means.mean(), means.std(), stats.skew(means))
print(population.std() / np.sqrt(n))

steps.do: Run the file.
steps.see: A population with skew about 2; sample means centred near 10 with an SD near 1.8, close to sigma / sqrt(30), and much less skewed.

steps.do: Change n to 120 and rerun: the SD of the means halves, and their skew shrinks further.
Put a breakpoint on the print line after the means are made, debug the file, and open Evaluate Expression to look at the means.
steps.code: np.percentile(means, [2.5, 97.5])
steps.see: The middle 95% of the sample means, about 6.8 to 13.9: not quite symmetric around 10, because a little skew remains at n = 30.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals
objectives: Build a confidence interval for a mean with the t distribution
Interpret a confidence interval correctly
key_points: A confidence interval for a mean is the estimate plus or minus a margin of error: a critical value times the standard error. stats.t.interval(0.95, n - 1, loc=mean, scale=sem) computes a 95% interval.
The t distribution replaces the normal when the population SD is estimated from the sample. It has heavier tails, and gets closer to the normal as the degrees of freedom, n - 1, grow.

95% describes the method, not one interval: if the sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true mean. Any single interval either contains it or doesn't.
Intervals get wider with more variable data, smaller samples or more confidence: a 99% interval from the same data is wider than a 95% one.

Coverage rests on assumptions: a random sample of independent values, and a sampling distribution close to normal. With skewed data and small samples, the real coverage can fall a little short of 95%.

walkthrough.title: Build intervals, then test the method by simulation

steps.do: In a new file, intervals.py, build a 95% and a 99% interval for the mean delivery time.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

minutes = pd.read_csv("deliveries.csv")["minutes"]
mean, sem = minutes.mean(), stats.sem(minutes)
print(stats.t.interval(0.95, len(minutes) - 1, loc=mean, scale=sem))
print(stats.t.interval(0.99, len(minutes) - 1, loc=mean, scale=sem))

steps.do: Run the file.
steps.see: About 26.72 to 30.46 minutes, and a wider 26.12 to 31.07 for 99%.

steps.do: Put the caret on interval and open its documentation to see what each argument means.
Test the method: make the skewed population from the last lesson, draw 1,000 samples of 30, build a 95% interval from each, and count how many contain the true mean.
steps.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
population = rng.exponential(scale=10, size=100_000)
n = 30
hits = 0
for _ in range(1_000):
    sample = rng.choice(population, size=n)
    low, high = stats.t.interval(0.95, n - 1, loc=sample.mean(), scale=stats.sem(sample))
    hits += low <= population.mean() <= high
print(hits)

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: Somewhere around 920 of 1,000: a little under 95%, because the population is skewed and the samples are small. Set n = 120 and rerun: the count moves close to 950.

lessons.title: Hypothesis tests and p-values
objectives: Set up null and alternative hypotheses
Run a t-test or a chi-square test and interpret its p-value
key_points: A hypothesis test starts from a null hypothesis, such as no difference between groups, and asks how surprising the data would be if it were true; the alternative hypothesis is what you conclude if the null is rejected.
The p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value means the data would be unusual if the null were true.
If the p-value is below a significance level chosen in advance, often 0.05, you reject the null. Rejecting a true null is a type I error; failing to reject a false one is a type II error.
stats.ttest_1samp(x, popmean=25) compares a mean with a fixed value; Welch's test, stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False), compares two groups' means without assuming they have equal variances.
stats.chi2_contingency(table) tests whether two categorical variables are related. It needs counts, not percentages, and expected counts of about 5 or more in each cell.

walkthrough.title: Run tests in the Python Console

steps.do: In the Python Console, test the claim that deliveries take 25 minutes on average.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
df = pd.read_csv("deliveries.csv")
stats.ttest_1samp(df["minutes"], popmean=25)
steps.see: A t statistic of about 3.80 and a p-value of about 0.0002: the data would be very surprising if the true mean were 25.

steps.do: Build the table of lateness (more than 35 minutes) by zone, and test it.
steps.code:
df["late"] = df["minutes"] > 35
table = pd.crosstab(df["zone"], df["late"])
result = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
result.statistic, result.pvalue, result.dof
steps.see: About 7.68, 0.0215 and 2 degrees of freedom.

steps.do: Check the assumption behind the chi-square test: the expected counts.
steps.code: result.expected_freq
steps.see: All 6.7 or more, so the test is reasonable here.

steps.do: Open the variables pane, right-click table and choose View as DataFrame: 12 of the 40 south deliveries were late, against 4 in each other zone.
Send a test from an editor file to the console: select the lines and use Execute Selection in Python Console.

lessons.title: The traps in p-values
objectives: Explain what a p-value does not tell you
Guard against multiple testing, low power and confusing significance with importance
key_points: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and 1 - p is not the probability that your idea is right.
Statistically significant doesn't mean important: with enough data a tiny difference gets a small p-value. Report the size of an effect and its confidence interval, not just p.
Not significant doesn't mean no effect: power, the chance that a study detects an effect that is really there, is low in small studies, so they can miss real differences.

With 20 tests at the 5% level and nothing really going on, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 - 0.95^20, about 0.64. Plan tests in advance, or adjust: the Bonferroni correction divides 0.05 by the number of tests.
Trying analyses until one gives p < 0.05, stopping the moment it does, or reporting only the tests that worked (p-hacking) produces findings that don't replicate.

walkthrough.title: See false positives and low power by simulation

steps.do: In a new file, traps.py, run 1,000 t-tests on pairs of samples from the same distribution, where the null hypothesis is true.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
false_positives = sum(
    stats.ttest_ind(rng.normal(0, 1, 30), rng.normal(0, 1, 30)).pvalue < 0.05
    for _ in range(1_000)
)
print(false_positives)

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: Around 50: about 5% of tests are significant when nothing is going on.

steps.do: Now give one group a real difference of 0.6 SD, with 20 in each group, and count how often the test detects it.
Rerun.
steps.see: A little under 500: with 20 per group, a real effect of 0.6 SD is missed about as often as it's found. The power is under 50%.

steps.do: Select the second sum(...) expression and extract it into a function, then give the function a parameter for the group size and try 50 per group.

lab.title: Intervals and tests on real questions
lab.goal: See the central limit theorem in a simulation, then answer three questions with a confidence interval and hypothesis tests: are deliveries slower than promised, does fertiliser change yields, and does lateness depend on the zone?
setup: Your PyCharm project with pandas and SciPy installed (SciPy 1.11 or later)
Download inference.py and fertiliser_trial.csv into the project, next to deliveries.csv

steps.do: Open inference.py. Part 1 makes the population for you; draw 2,000 samples of 30, keep their means, and print their mean, SD and skew, then the SD that sigma / sqrt(n) predicts.
Part 2: build a 95% confidence interval for the mean delivery time with stats.t.interval.
Part 3: test whether the mean delivery time differs from the promised 25 minutes with stats.ttest_1samp.
Part 4: compare yields with and without fertiliser with Welch's t-test, and get the 95% interval for the difference with result.confidence_interval(0.95).
Part 5: test whether lateness (more than 35 minutes) is related to the zone with stats.chi2_contingency, and print the smallest expected count.

Run inference.py.

"""From samples to conclusions: the central limit theorem, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests."""

# 6. Multiple testing

modules.title: Relationships and experiments
modules.summary: Measure how two variables move together with correlation and simple linear regression, then run the experiment that data science uses most: the A/B test.

lessons.title: Correlation
objectives: Measure the strength of a linear relationship with Pearson's r
Explain why correlation doesn't show causation
key_points: Pearson's correlation coefficient, r, measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship, from -1 (perfectly negative) through 0 (no linear relationship) to +1 (perfectly positive).
r captures only straight-line relationships: a strong curved relationship can have r near 0, so look at the data before trusting r.
Spearman's rank correlation applies the same idea to the ranks of the values, so it measures any relationship that keeps going up or keeps going down, and outliers affect it less.
stats.pearsonr(x, y) and stats.spearmanr(x, y) return the coefficient and a p-value for the null hypothesis of no correlation; df.corr(numeric_only=True) gives every pair of numeric columns at once.

Correlation is not causation: two variables can move together because a third drives both (confounding), by chance, or because the effect runs the other way. Randomised experiments are how causes are established.

steps.do: Download fertiliser_trial.csv from module 3's lab if you don't have it, open the Python Console and load it.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
trial = pd.read_csv("fertiliser_trial.csv")
trial.corr(numeric_only=True)
steps.see: A table with r = 0.734 between rainfall and yield.

steps.do: Get Pearson's and Spearman's coefficients with their p-values.
steps.code:
stats.pearsonr(trial["rainfall_mm"], trial["yield_t_ha"])
stats.spearmanr(trial["rainfall_mm"], trial["yield_t_ha"])
steps.see: r = 0.734 and rho = 0.737, both with tiny p-values.

steps.do: See r miss a perfect curved relationship.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.arange(-5, 6)
stats.pearsonr(x, x ** 2)
steps.see: r is 0 (to rounding), although y is completely determined by x.

steps.do: In the variables pane, right-click trial and choose View as DataFrame, then sort by rainfall_mm to see the relationship in the rows themselves.

lessons.title: Simple linear regression
objectives: Fit a straight line by least squares and interpret its slope and intercept
Judge a fit with R squared and residuals, and know where predictions stop being safe
key_points: Simple linear regression fits y = intercept + slope x x by least squares: the line that makes the sum of the squared vertical distances from the points to the line, the residuals, as small as possible.
The slope is the average change in y for each one-unit increase in x. The intercept is the predicted y when x is 0, which may lie far outside the data and mean nothing in practice.
R squared, which in simple regression is r squared, is the share of the variation in y that the line accounts for; the rest is left in the residuals.
stats.linregress(x, y) returns the slope, the intercept, rvalue, the p-value for the null hypothesis of a zero slope, and the standard error of the slope.

Check the residuals for patterns, such as a curve or a spread that grows with x, and predict only within the range of x in the data: extrapolating assumes the line carries on where you have no evidence.

walkthrough.title: Fit a line and examine the residuals

steps.do: In a new file, regression.py, fit yield against rainfall.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

trial = pd.read_csv("fertiliser_trial.csv")
fit = stats.linregress(trial["rainfall_mm"], trial["yield_t_ha"])
print(fit)

steps.do: Run the file.
steps.see: slope about 0.00321, intercept about 0.803, rvalue about 0.734, and a tiny p-value.

steps.do: Add the residuals, and a prediction for 600 mm of rain. Extract the prediction into a variable with a clear name.
steps.code:
predicted = fit.intercept + fit.slope * trial["rainfall_mm"]
trial["residual"] = trial["yield_t_ha"] - predicted
print(fit.intercept + fit.slope * 600)
steps.see: About 2.73 t/ha predicted at 600 mm.

steps.do: Put a breakpoint after the residuals are added, debug the file and view trial as a DataFrame, sorted by residual: are the fertilised plots mostly above the line?
Evaluate the mean residual for each group while paused.
steps.code: trial.groupby("fertiliser")["residual"].mean()
steps.see: Positive for fertilised plots and negative for the others: rainfall doesn't explain everything.

lessons.title: A/B tests
objectives: Design an A/B test that can answer its question
Analyse an A/B test with a two-proportion test and a confidence interval
key_points: An A/B test splits users at random between two versions and compares an outcome, such as the share who sign up. Randomisation makes the groups alike in everything but the version, so a difference can be put down to the version or to chance.
Before it starts, decide the metric, the smallest difference worth detecting, the significance level and the sample size; the sample size grows fast as the difference you want to detect shrinks.

A two-proportion z-test compares two conversion rates using the pooled rate under the null hypothesis; it gives the same p-value as a chi-square test of the 2 x 2 table without the continuity correction.
Report the difference with its confidence interval, such as +2.0 percentage points (95% CI +0.4 to +3.6), so readers can see how large or small the real effect could plausibly be.

Checking the results every day and stopping as soon as p < 0.05 (peeking) pushes the false-positive rate well above 5%. Fix the sample size in advance, or use a method designed for sequential testing.

walkthrough.title: Analyse an A/B test, then plan the next one

steps.do: In a new file, ab_test.py, enter the results: 2,400 visitors saw each sign-up page, and 192 signed up on page A and 240 on page B.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

n_a, n_b, x_a, x_b = 2400, 2400, 192, 240
p_a, p_b = x_a / n_a, x_b / n_b
pooled = (x_a + x_b) / (n_a + n_b)
z = (p_b - p_a) / np.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / n_a + 1 / n_b))
print(p_a, p_b, z, 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z)))

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: 0.08, 0.1, z about 2.42 and p about 0.0155.

steps.do: Check the answer with chi2_contingency, turning the continuity correction off. Use Parameter Info to find the correction argument.
steps.code: stats.chi2_contingency([[x_a, n_a - x_a], [x_b, n_b - x_b]], correction=False)
steps.see: chi2 about 5.86, which is z squared, and the same p-value.

steps.do: Work out how many visitors per group the next test needs to detect a change from 8% to 10% with 80% power at the 5% level.
steps.code:
z_alpha, z_beta = stats.norm.ppf(0.975), stats.norm.ppf(0.80)
print((z_alpha + z_beta) ** 2 * (0.08 * 0.92 + 0.10 * 0.90) / 0.02 ** 2)
steps.see: About 3,210 per group.

steps.do: Rerun after changing the target to 8% -> 9%, and see the sample size roughly quadruple.

# TODO: print it rounded up:  Visitors needed per group: ...

hints: fit.rvalue ** 2 is R squared; f'{fit.slope * 100:+.2f}' prints the slope per 100 mm with its sign.
Work in proportions, then multiply by 100 for percentage points: (p_b - p_a) * 100 is +2.0.
The interval's margin is 1.96 times the unpooled standard error, sqrt(p_a * (1 - p_a) / n_a + p_b * (1 - p_b) / n_b).

project.title: Analyse a field trial of SMS weather advice
project.brief: A farmers' cooperative piloted a service that texts weather advice to farmers (the data are made up). Of 120 farmers across three regions, 60 were chosen at random to get the texts for a season, and the other 60 carried on as before; sms_trial.csv records each farmer's group, region, the season's rainfall on their plot and their yield. The cooperative wants to know whether to pay for the service for everyone. Analyse the trial in PyCharm with pandas and SciPy: describe the data, check that randomisation balanced the groups, estimate the difference in yield with a confidence interval and a test, look at how rainfall relates to yield, and write a short report for people who aren't statisticians that says what the trial shows, what it doesn't, and what you recommend.
deliverables: analysis.py: loads sms_trial.csv and prints every number your report uses
Descriptive statistics of yield and rainfall for each group, and for each region
A check that the two groups had similar rainfall, with a test or an interval
The difference in mean yield between the groups, with a 95% confidence interval, a test and an effect size
A simple regression of yield on rainfall, with its slope and R squared interpreted
report.md: a one-page report with your findings, the limitations and pitfalls, and a recommendation

rubric.name: Describing the data
rubric.description: Means, medians, SDs and counts by group and region are right and clearly presented; outliers are looked for and handled with a reason.

rubric.name: The right tests, run correctly
rubric.description: Welch's t-test (or an equally sound choice) compares the groups; the randomisation check is done; assumptions such as independence and the shape of the data are considered.

rubric.name: Intervals and effect sizes
rubric.description: The difference is reported in tonnes per hectare with a 95% confidence interval and an effect size, not as a p-value alone.

rubric.name: Regression
rubric.description: The regression's slope, intercept and R squared are right and explained in plain words, with residuals checked and no predictions outside the data's range.

rubric.name: Interpretation and pitfalls
rubric.description: The report separates what the trial shows from what it doesn't (one season, one cooperative), avoids p-value traps such as testing every region separately without saying so, and makes a recommendation that follows from the evidence.

rubric.name: Reproducible code
rubric.description: analysis.py runs from start to finish on the data file, with clear names and comments, and prints the numbers the report quotes.

project.submit: Paste analysis.py, its output and report.md.
